title: What would make you trust a multi-exchange crypto trading interface?
author: sepegar_cm

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the unknown state is the one that earns trust. show it loudly and never let the UI guess it into filled or rejected, because the worst story people tell is a rejected order that actually filled after a timeout.

replies.author: sepegar_cm
replies.body: Good point. I’ve been using it for my own fast trades for about a year, so I’ve focused heavily on making entries and exits appear almost instantly, in sync with the exchange. But you’re right—a timeout should show as “verifying,” not “rejected,” until the actual order and position are confirmed.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: a year of your own fast trades is a better test than most of these get. I'd also count how often "verifying" shows up per exchange, because one venue timing out ten times more than the others tells you something before a user does.

replies.author: sepegar_cm
replies.body: That’s a smart idea. Tracking timeouts per exchange would help identify API issues before users notice them. I’ll add this to the monitoring side.

replies.author: filwu
replies.body: For the per-exchange monitor, could you show both timeout count and the number of order requests over the same reporting window? Hypothetically, 10 timeouts out of 10,000 requests is 0.1%, while 1 out of 100 is 1%: ten times the count, but one-tenth the rate. I'd also label whether retries count as separate requests, so the denominator stays interpretable. That would make the venue comparison much more useful than raw counts alone.

comments.author: ciaranwalsh96
comments.body:
Beyond order-state handling, I’d need the security model to be inspectable. The key should be trade-only and withdrawal-disabled, with IP allowlisting where the venue supports it. The app should document where keys are encrypted, how they can be rotated or revoked, and ensure they never appear in client logs.



I’d also want a trust-building path: start read-only, then testnet, then one minimum-size canary order. For each order, show the exchange order ID and a timestamped reconciliation trail, plus an exportable audit log. A prominent kill switch that blocks new orders, requests cancellation where possible, and tells me exactly which exchange keys to revoke would matter more to me than a fast UI.



Finally, publish the failure drills: exchange timeout, duplicate retry, partial fill, app restart and stale balance. Seeing the expected safe behavior for each would give me more confidence than a generic security claim.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I'd want to see four things before connecting a key. Where the keys are stored and who can read them (ideally encrypted so even you can't see them), plus a clear statement that withdrawals can never be enabled on the key and an IP whitelist so a leaked key is useless elsewhere. Then an audit log I can see myself of every request the app sent and every response it got, so when something looks wrong I can prove what happened. The "unknown" order state is the most important one in your list, so I'd want to know what the app does with it: it should never retry blindly, and it should show me the exchange's own status before offering another action. Last, what happens when your service is down, because the exchange side should keep working through the exchange's own app and my stops should live at the exchange, not in your app. Cymetica's Exchange Connections page is one place to see how strategies get linked to exchanges.

replies.author: sepegar_cm
replies.body:
That’s very close to how I’ve designed it. Keys are trade-only with withdrawals disabled, and IP whitelisting is used where the exchange supports it. Orders and stops live on the exchange, so users can still manage everything through the exchange’s own app if Sepegar goes down.

For an unknown order state, the system checks the actual exchange status instead of blindly sending the order again. Requests and responses are already logged internally; making that audit trail visible to each user is one of the next improvements. I also agree that documenting encryption and key access clearly is essential for trust.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That covers the main points. One tip when you publish the security notes: write the key-handling part as a short plain-language page (where keys live, who can read them, what happens if you're breached) and keep it separate from the marketing, since that's the page careful users will go to first. Thanks for the clear answers.

replies.author: sepegar_cm
replies.body: That’s a good point. I’ll create a separate security page covering key storage, access, permissions and breach procedures in plain language, without marketing around it. Thanks for the useful feedback.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Sounds like a good plan. A plain security page tends to build more trust than any feature list, so I'll leave it there. Thanks for the open discussion.
